paragraphs.text: Kramer et al. (1990) and Kwiatkowski et al. (1991) described idiopathic torsion dystonia as a neurologic disorder of sustained, involuntary muscle contractions. These often cause twisting and repetitive movements of the limbs, trunk, and/or neck and can progress to abnormal postures. Most familial forms show autosomal dominant inheritance with reduced penetrance. Ozelius et al. (1997) described early-onset torsion dystonia as a movement disorder that begins in childhood. Its symptoms were believed to result from altered neuronal communication in the basal ganglia. Risch et al. (2007) noted that the DYT1 GAG deletion is a major cause of early-onset dystonia, but only 30% of mutation carriers express clinical disease.

paragraphs.text: Bressman et al. (1994) studied 174 Ashkenazi Jewish individuals with idiopathic torsion dystonia. Using a DYT1-associated haplotype of 9q34 markers (D9S62, D9S63, and ASS), they classified 90 individuals as carriers, 70 as noncarriers, and 14 as ambiguous. Mean age at onset was significantly lower in carriers than in noncarriers (12.5 +/- 8.2 vs 36.5 +/- 16.4 years). In 94% of carriers, symptoms began in a limb, with arm and leg affected equally often. Onset in the neck (3.3%) or larynx (2.2%) was rare.

paragraphs.text: Calakos et al. (2010) reported a man in his fifth decade of life who had had involuntary jaw movements and grimacing for 3 years, consistent with oromandibular dystonia. Examination showed cogwheel tone without rigidity, a mild action/postural tremor of the upper extremities, and absent Achilles reflexes. Brain MRI and laboratory studies were normal. paragraphs.text: Askenasy et al. (1980) studied 13 Ashkenazi Jewish patients with torsion dystonia of various origins, together with their families. Serum dopamine-beta-hydroxylase (DBH) activity was significantly higher in patients and their relatives than in controls, particularly in the childhood-onset group. Jewish origin, dominant inheritance, slow progression, and axial distribution were each not specific for elevated serum DBH activity. An intravenous injection of 20 mg metoclopramide did not change serum DBH activity in 12 patients with torsion dystonia or in 17 relatives. In 1 patient with symptomatic dystonia and in 2 of her maternal relatives, who had different fathers, serum DBH activity doubled or tripled after the injection. The authors suggested that a metoclopramide-induced rise in serum DBH activity in relatives of patients with torsion dystonia indicates a genetic predisposition.

paragraphs.text: Hornykiewicz et al. (1986) examined the brains of 2 patients with generalized childhood-onset dystonia musculorum deformans after death. Histology showed no important changes in the basal ganglia, cerebral cortex, higher brainstem nuclei, locus ceruleus, or raphe nuclei. Choline acetyltransferase activity and levels of GABA and glutamic acid in the cortex and basal ganglia were within the control range. Norepinephrine concentrations were markedly and consistently decreased in the lateral and posterior hypothalamus, mamillary body, subthalamic nucleus, and locus ceruleus. Serotonin was subnormal in the dorsal raphe nucleus. Dopamine was low in the nucleus accumbens in both cases and in the striatum in 1 of the 2 cases. Norepinephrine, serotonin, and 5-HIAA were raised in several other regions.

paragraphs.text: Zilber et al. (1984) analyzed idiopathic torsion dystonia (ITD) in 47 Israeli Jewish patients. Assuming that all cases fit one genetic model, X-linked and simple autosomal recessive models did not fit the data well. An autosomal dominant model with low penetrance could account for the observations and gave an estimated ITD gene frequency of 3 to 4 per 100,000 in European Jews. Multifactorial inheritance was also possible. The authors cautioned that it may be inappropriate to assume that all cases share the same genetic basis, or even that all are inherited. Fathers of isolated cases were older than expected, and on this basis the authors suggested that some isolated cases may have been new mutations.

The variant was not present in 800 population controls (1,600 chromosomes). In BHK cells expressing EGFP-tagged TOR1A, inclusions formed in 44% of cells expressing F205I, 79% of cells expressing deltaE, and 10% of cells expressing wildtype protein. The F205I inclusions were larger than the deltaE inclusions. They colocalized mostly with the ER marker KDEL (96%) rather than with the nuclear envelope marker lamin B1 (19%), whereas deltaE inclusions colocalized with lamin B1 (89%). The authors concluded that F205I impairs TOR1A function, probably through a pathophysiology that differs from that of deltaE, and that the variant may contribute to the expression of dystonia.

paragraphs.text: In a man in his fifth decade of life with late-onset focal (oromandibular) dystonia, Calakos et al. (2010) identified a novel heterozygous c.613T-A mutation in exon 3 of the TOR1A gene, resulting in a phe205-to-ile (F205I) substitution at a highly conserved residue in a beta strand of the AAA domain. The variant was not found in 1,600 control chromosomes. In BHK cells, the F205I mutant formed inclusions in 44% of cells, compared with 79% for deltaE and 10% for wildtype. These inclusions were larger than deltaE inclusions and colocalized mostly with the ER marker KDEL rather than with the nuclear envelope marker lamin B1. The authors suggested that F205I impairs TOR1A function through a mechanism different from that of deltaE, which may reflect the milder clinical phenotype.

checks.explanation: Zygosity (heterozygous) is not stated in the paper.

checks.claim: The man with the TOR1A F205I mutation was in his fifth decade of life.

checks.claim: The TOR1A F205I variant was not found in 1,600 control chromosomes.

checks.claim: In BHK cells, the TOR1A F205I mutant formed inclusions in 44% of cells, compared with 79% for deltaE and 10% for wildtype.
